Getty Images Political observers are watching the Texas gubernatorial election for signs of an artificial intelligence data center backlash in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, and prediction market traders see growing odds of the Democratic candidate pulling off an upset. Gov. Greg Abbott , a Republican seeking a fourth term, has a 60% chance of beating Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, according to speculators on platform Kalshi. Hinojosa's odds to win have jumped from 8% in mid-July to 40% on Monday, with many of those gains coming in recent weeks as a series of polls have shown the race to be tightening . Hinojosa is seeking to be the first Democratic governor in Texas in more than 30 years. In November 2025, Abbott touted a $40 billion investment by Google — which included bringing three new data centers to the state — by saying that Texas will be the "epicenter of AI development." But Abbott has changed his tune as voters' opinion of data centers has soured over the past year. Abbott in August ordered an audit of data centers that sought to connect to the state's grid, and then in September halted the approval of all data center-related permits until an audit of the existing waitlist is conducted. Hinojosa is running on an immediate data center moratorium until the legislature puts guardrails on the industry, according to her campaign website. headlines.article_text: Apple Q4 2026 earnings live updates: Ternus' first call Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu watch now VIDEO 3:49 03:49 Needham's Laura Martin on Apple: 'We need to watch what's happening in China' Squawk on the Street Apple reports fiscal fourth-quarter earnings after the bell on Monday, with new CEO John Ternus expected to address Wall Street in a meaningful way for the first time. Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG. EPS: $1.99 Revenue: $113.39 billion Revenue is expected to increase 11% from $102.5 billion a year earlier. Analysts project $56.59 billion in iPhone sales for the quarter. Wall Street is closely watching iPhone revenue because the report will include eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales. But Apple's new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, didn't hit store shelves until the quarter was over, and Apple didn't announce a new entry-level iPhone 18. Apple also raised prices on iPhones by $100, which may have hurt demand in the quarter. Monday's earnings call, set to start at 5 p.m. ET, will be the first with Ternus at the helm. Investors want to hear from him about the company's plans in China after its AI software got approved, as well as the slew of recent product launches and how the company continues to grapple with global shortages of memory and flash storage. Read more CNBC Apple news Apple brings touch to the Mac, ending decades-old stance on touchscreen laptops Apple stock has become an anti-AI trade. Here’s why Apple responds to user reports of broken iPhone Duo screens 42 Min Ago Barclays stays underweight Apple, remains 'cautious on the stock' Analysts at Barclays wrote in an earnings preview over the weekend that they "remain cautious on the stock given iPhone uncertainties this cycle, limited monetization of AI, and renewed fears on the App Store." The firm has an underweight rating on the shares, and said the "pricing benefits AAPL has been enjoying from the memory backdrop due to its scale and preferential pricing are fading." —Ari Levy 1 Hour Ago Concerns about gross margin watch now VIDEO 1:09 01:09 Bank of America forecasts a much weaker December quarter for Apple Fast Money Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan said on Friday that his team had a "conservative outlook" on earnings because of gross margin concerns and price increases. The analyst pointed out that Apple's gross margins in the September quarter will be boosted by a positive impact from tariff refunds, and that margins could drop in the coming quarters. Apple reported a gross margin of 49.3% in its June quarter, but warned that it would be between 47.5% and 48% in the September period. "Investor focus will likely be on component cost inflation, durability of gross margin and services revenue growth," Mohan wrote in the note. Bank of America maintains a Buy rating on the stock and a price target of $370. — Kif Leswing 2 Hours Ago Tough market for smartphones and PCs due to memory shortage watch now VIDEO 6:17 06:17 Intel faces a 'multi-quarter' issue balancing PC weakness with AI data-center gains: Vivek Arya Squawk Box Apple is competing in a smartphone and PC market that has "never been worse," IDC's Ryan Reith told CNBC. Consumer electronics companies everywhere are grappling with surging prices for computer parts, including memory and flash storage that's used in every smartphone and laptop. Intel on Friday had its worst day on the stock market since the 1970s, dropping 29%, after the company cited PC softness for a disappointing forecast . Many companies have responded to component shortages by raising prices or reducing specifications for current devices. Consumers are holding onto their old computers for far longer, driving sales down. IDC says the smartphone market is set to drop nearly 17% this year based on shipments. PCs could be down 11%. Apple isn't immune. The company raised prices on almost all of its products since executives warned over the summer that the market was in a "thousand year flood." — Kif Leswing 3 Hours Ago No iPhone Duo this quarter, but some iPhone 18 sales watch now VIDEO 2:07 02:07 Apple ramps iPhone Duo production as early screen failures emerge Squawk Box Asia Apple's new $2,000 foldable phone won't have any sales for the quarter, which ended last month. While Apple and Ternus announced new iPhones on Sept. 9, the foldable Duo didn't go on sale until a month later, on Oct 23. Some analysts have theorized that Apple's most committed fans may have been waiting to see the Duo come out before buying it. There will be a few weeks of sales from the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which went on sale on Sept. 18. — Kif Leswing 4 Hours Ago Ternus has been everywhere John Ternus, chief executive officer of Apple Inc., speaks during an event in Los Angeles, California, US, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Kyle Grillot | Bloomberg | Getty Images Apple investors and customers are still getting to know Ternus, but since he took over for Tim Cook on Sept. 1, the new CEO has embraced his new role as the face of the iPhone company. Ternus' first major appearance came nine days into his tenure, when he unveiled the iPhone Duo at Apple's headquarters. A week later, he was walking the red carpet at the Emmys. He then flew to New York, where he opened the doors at an Apple store to commemorate the new iPhone Pro going on sale. He also went to Austin, Texas, this month to kick off sales of the iPhone Duo, and appeared at an elementary school and an F1 race while on the trip. And he's had a busy media schedule, including an appearance on the cover of Time magazine. Last week, Ternus continued a new style of Apple product introduction in unveiling the first MacBook with a touchscreen using a format he first tried out in the spring. That's when Apple launched its low-cost MacBook Neo. Ternus addressed a crowd of media and analysts, giving a five minute speech interspersed with a few short videos. Investors will get their first in-depth look at Ternus on Monday. He's been on the past few calls, but hasn't given extended remarks, and largely deferred to Cook when asked questions. — Kif Leswing 4 Hours Ago Stock is Wall Street's favorite among the megacaps Apple vs. Nasdaq this year Heading into its earnings report, Apple has emerged as the preferred megacap tech stock on Wall Street. The shares are up 27% this year as of Friday's close, by far outpacing Apple's leading peers. It's also the last among the group (other than Nvidia, which reports next month) to issue quarterly earnings. Investors weren't kind to the hyperscalers over the past two weeks, scrutinizing their hefty expenses and dwindling cash flows. Apple is in a much different category as the iPhone maker has avoided running up huge capital expenditures bills, taking a more measured approach to its AI investing. —Ari Levy

headlines.article_text: Trump Accounts to get SpaceX shares from Shotwell in December Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Eligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock from President and COO Gwynne Shotwell in December. The donation will go directly into about 2 million investment accounts of kids ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less. Elon Musk in October separately pledged to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX, which could come via Trump Accounts sometime in 2027. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell celebrates with family and other SpaceX employees at the Nasdaq Marketsite in in New York after the SpaceX initial public offering on June 12, 2026. Spencer Platt | Getty Images News | Getty Images Eligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock next month, according to an X post on Friday. "Robert and I are thrilled that our gift of over 2 million shares of SpaceX stock will be distributed to children's Trump accounts in December!" President and COO Gwynne Shotwell wrote in the post. The gift from Shotwell and her husband will provide a share apiece to around 2 million Trump Accounts holders ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less, or in ZIP codes with too few residents for a median family income to be reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. These families should receive a notice by Monday, Shotwell wrote on X. "In a few weeks, an additional gift will be finalized for eligible 11 to 17-year-old children in military families serving overseas, children in foster care, and more children whose MFI is $90,000 or less living in counties near our home in the great state of Texas," she also wrote. Parents or guardians can check eligibility for the donation through Invest America, a nonprofit advocacy group, and track account activity with the Trump Accounts app . In a separate funding announcement in October, Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which may also come via Trump Accounts . The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds . headlines.article_text: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds, it said in a filing. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. In this article ORCL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled more than 6% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. Oracle's one-day performance The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.267%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 296, up 270% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026 While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out." — CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting. In this article MRVL LITE Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:41 04:41 Marvell CEO Matt Murphy on Lumentum deal: We're creating the 'category leader in AI connectivity' Squawk on the Street Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 8% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank 13%. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology. Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm.
